Thought: Evaluation/benchmark paper: 100 OMIM phenotype entries drafted from exactly the cited papers by one model (Claude Opus 5.5) under six strategies, scored against fixed fact lists split from OMIM allelic-variant text in ClinVar. The cleanest result is the within-paper manipulation: hiding the full text drops coverage from 79.8% to 36.1%, an effect far above any judge or replicate noise. The strategy comparison is a near-null (three reading strategies within 0.7 points; replicate-noise half-width 1.0) in a regime (2-12 refs, 19% full text, fits one prompt) where direct reading is expected to do well, and stated-fact coverage sits at a 94% ceiling, so the benchmark has little power to separate designs. The reference covers only ~24% of what a draft says. Every judgement (audit, fact coverage, 'stated in text') comes from the writer's model family with no human check. Because all strategies share the model, self-preference matters less for the relative comparisons, but absolute levels and the 'stated' attribution are unvalidated. The released-system comparison (10 and 4 entries, non-default settings, systems not repaired, STORM blocked) and the second-round experiments (cut to a third of the design) are underpowered. The paper is unusually honest and careful (completion treated as an outcome, symmetric handling of stopped replies, fixed fact lists, replicate noise, planted-error audit stress test), but the headline finding is expected, the ML takeaway is modest and domain-specific, and the prose is very dense. Borderline; leaning reject at the ICLR bar.
Summary: The paper builds a controlled benchmark for evidence-grounded knowledge-base writing. It uses 100 OMIM phenotype entries, each with 2-12 cited references (515 papers, 19% readable in full via open access), and drafts each entry from its header and exactly the cited papers, with the causal gene withheld. One model writes all drafts under a shared set of guards (ontology-candidate search, HGNC normalisation, mandatory citation), a shared claim-level audit with one repair round, and shared scoring. Strategies: direct reading (all papers in one prompt), an agentic curator with read/search tools, an evidence graph and a case table (extract then write), recall-then-verify, and a memory-only control. Add-ons: second-hand evidence, a reconciled case database and a learned curation guide. The primary endpoint is coverage of fixed fact lists (6,652 facts) split once from OMIM's allelic-variant descriptions deposited in ClinVar. Secondary measures cover HPO synopsis terms, variants, causal gene and inheritance. Main findings: (i) hiding full text for the same papers lowers coverage from 79.8% to 36.1%; (ii) direct reading, the agentic curator and the evidence graph are within about a point of one another and convey 93.6-94.4% of facts the supplied text is judged to state, while the case-table-first implementation trails; (iii) memory-only drafting conveys about 15% overall and little for recent entries; (iv) on 10 and 4 entries, released PaperQA2 and GraphRAG pipelines convey fewer facts than direct reading at higher cost, and STORM could not run because the model's safety filter stopped its prompts; (v) the audit catches citation swaps, moved sentences and blunt value changes, but by construction cannot see over-citation or omissions, and rarely catches broadened claims. Further experiments cover padding with unrelated papers, large entries (all blocked by stopped replies), replicate noise and judge variation, and measurement lessons such as handling stopped replies symmetrically.
Strengths: The within-paper access manipulation (the same 46 entries, the same 2,120 fixed facts, full text hidden versus available) is a clean causal design. Its effect (+43.7 points; better in every entry but one tie) is far larger than any judge or replicate noise the authors measure, so the headline claim that access bounds agreement is well supported for this regime.

Strong experimental hygiene that many LLM-pipeline comparisons lack. Model, sources, guards, audit and scoring are held fixed. Fact lists are split once without sight of any draft, so denominators do not adapt to drafts. Completion is treated as an outcome, with a symmetric rule and an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis. Replicate noise (three replicates on 30 entries) and judge variation (three judgings) are reported beside bootstrap intervals.

The paper is unusually candid about its own measurement pitfalls. Asymmetric handling of stopped replies produced a spurious 2.1-point difference, larger than the true differences between strategies. The frameshift naming bug is disclosed and fixed, per-draft fact splitting is reported to inflate levels by 2-5 points, and the paper notes which conclusions rest on 4-10 entries. Section 5's 'measurement lessons' are practical and transferable to other LLM-pipeline benchmarks.

The attribution analyses (where missed facts went, where conveyed facts came from, and coverage restricted to facts the supplied text states) decompose the gap to the reference into access and reading failures. This is more informative than a single coverage number.

The audit characterisation is useful and sobering. The planted-error classes show that a best-verdict-over-cited-papers audit cannot detect added irrelevant citations or omissions, and rarely detects broadened claims. The second-hand-evidence analysis shows that an audit against what the writer saw can pass claims the full text contradicts. These are concrete, actionable insights for anyone deploying claim-level verification.
Contamination is addressed empirically: a memory-only control by creation era, plus a held-out set of entries created in 2026, used in no development, on which the ordering replicates.

Reproducibility is high: all drafts, verdicts and scores are to be released per entry, along with the harness. Reference-building is limited to public sources, licensing of curator text is respected, and full token and cost accounting is given.
Weaknesses: No human validation of any judgement. Atomic claim splitting, audit verdicts, fact present/partial/absent marks, the 'stated in the supplied text' attribution and variant-name matching are all made by the writer's model family. Because every strategy shares the model, self-preference bias matters less for the relative comparisons. However, the absolute levels (e.g., 94% of stated facts conveyed, 1.7% of conveyed facts in no supplied text) and the 'stated' restriction underlying Section 4.3 are unvalidated. Re-judging agreement (95.7%) measures self-consistency, not accuracy. For a benchmark paper, even a modest expert-annotated sample (e.g., a few hundred fact marks and 'stated' verdicts) would substantially strengthen the claims.

Single model, for both generation and judging. Whether 'strategy matters little' generalises to weaker or differently trained models, where structured intermediates or agents may matter more, is untested. The paper's own STORM failure and frequent safety-filter stops show that conclusions are entangled with idiosyncrasies of this model.

The strategy comparison has low discriminative power in the tested regime. Inputs are 2-12 references that fit one prompt and 81% of papers are abstract- or title-only, a regime in which direct reading is expected to do well. Stated-fact coverage is near a ceiling (94%; 95.5-97.1% on abstract-only papers, where most entries tie). Differences among the three leading strategies (<=0.7 points) are of the order of the replicate-noise half-width (1.0). As a benchmark, it therefore cannot separate designs except on the small full-text-heavy subset. The regime where strategies plausibly matter (large sets of relevant papers) could not be evaluated because every large entry was stopped.

The primary reference is narrow and indirect relative to the task. It consists of variant-centred allelic-variant paragraphs from gene entries, not the phenotype entries' narrative sections. Only about 24% of a direct-reading draft's statements have a counterpart in the reference, so roughly three quarters of each draft is evaluated only by the self-audit for fidelity, never for correctness or completeness. Strategies could differ substantially on that unscored portion (clinical description, organisation, synthesis across papers).

The headline finding is largely expected, as the authors acknowledge: curators wrote from full papers, and full text yields more than abstracts. The added value is the effect size within the same papers, but a 44-point gap from removing most of a paper's content is not surprising. The ML takeaways (strategy matters little when everything fits in context; audits by best verdict hide over-citation) are modest and partly known from the long-context vs. RAG and attribution literatures.

Possible memory-guided selection is not ruled out. The provenance analysis shows that conveyed facts are mostly stated in the supplied text. However, on older entries the model may know the OMIM entry and use memory to choose which stated facts to include, matching what curators wrote. This would inflate the 'reading strategies convey >90% of stated facts' figure without leaving a provenance trace. The decline in abstract-only coverage from 49.8% to 37.9% in the newest band is consistent with this. The stated-fact analysis (Table 2) is not reported for the newest band or the 2026 set.

The released-system comparison is too small and not like-for-like to support much. It covers 10 entries for PaperQA2 and 4 for GraphRAG (no test possible), with non-default settings forced by a local adapter, and PaperQA2 runs without its agent. Both systems answer six section questions rather than their intended task, and their drafts are not repaired while the strategies' are. STORM produced nothing. The appendix states that these second-round experiments were cut to about a third of their design before finishing. The abstract and conclusion still foreground this comparison.

Safety-filter stops cause non-random attrition. Seven of 100 main entries, 10 of 30 2026 entries, and all large entries are lost. If stops correlate with disease content (e.g., lethal, reproductive or child-related phenotypes), the compared set is a biased subsample. There is no analysis of which entries or papers are stopped, and the reasons are unobservable.

Statistical framing of the case-table-first result is borderline. The primary endpoint is not adjusted across the five comparisons against direct reading. The case-table interval excludes zero but its sign test gives p = 0.071. The 'matched ablation' changes two factors together and attributes the gain to extraction effort only by inference. The observational access-group analysis is confounded with creation date and journal, which the authors note.

Presentation is very dense. Nearly every sentence carries multiple caveats and numbers; heavy domain vocabulary (OMIM, ClinVar, HPO, MedGen, mim2gene, allelic-variant descriptions) is introduced quickly; and many key details live in 47 appendix tables. An ML reader will find it hard to extract the main message and the benchmark specification. A crisper main text, with fewer secondary results and a short worked example of an entry, its fact list and a scored draft, would help considerably.

Minor: the agentic curator's paper-opening behaviour is self-reported (tool calls not logged). The interface exposes no temperature or seed, so exact regeneration is impossible. Draft length is not controlled or analysed as a covariate of coverage.
Questions: Can you provide expert validation on a stratified sample? For example, have a clinical geneticist or biocurator mark a few hundred (fact, draft) coverage judgements, the corresponding 'stated in supplied text' verdicts, and a sample of audit verdicts, and report agreement with the model judge. This seems the single most important addition for a benchmark contribution.

Could you re-judge at least the 30-entry replicate subset with a judge from a different model family, and ideally regenerate it with a second writer model? This would show whether the near-tie among reading strategies, and the case-table deficit, are model-specific.

Is Table 2 (coverage restricted to stated vs. not-stated facts) reported for the newest creation band and for the 2026 entries? If stated-fact coverage stays near 94% there, that would largely rule out memory-guided selection of curator-salient facts as a driver of the 'reading conveys >90% of stated facts' result.

What is the minimum detectable paired difference on the primary endpoint at n = 93, given the observed paired SDs and replicate noise? Could you construct a harder, more discriminative subset (e.g., full-text-heavy entries, or facts stated only outside the abstract) on which strategies separate, so the benchmark remains useful as models improve?

What characterises the entries and papers where the safety filter stopped a reply (disease area, phenotype content, paper type)? Is attrition in the main comparison plausibly independent of strategy-relevant difficulty? Was any attempt made to run the large entries with another model, so the large-entry regime is not untested?

For the released systems, how much does the gap change if (a) the strategies' drafts are scored before the repair round, (b) PaperQA2 is run with its agent through a function-calling interface, and (c) each system is used for its intended output rather than six section questions? Since the hidden-full-text experiment suggests repair barely moves coverage, (a) should be cheap to report.

Does coverage correlate with draft length within strategies? Would a length-normalised or precision-aware endpoint (e.g., facts conveyed per statement, or penalising unsupported statements) change the ordering?

The reference covers about 24% of draft statements. Did you assess correctness, not just self-audited fidelity, of any sample of the remaining 76%, e.g., by checking against full text where available?

With five strategy comparisons against direct reading on the primary endpoint, does the case-table-first deficit survive a Holm adjustment across them? Could the matched ablation be split into its two component changes to remove the inference step?
Limitations: The authors' limitations section is thorough and candid (single model family; no human validation; narrow reference; reference list given; open-access text only; small second-round experiments; stopped replies).

Additional limitation to state explicitly: memory of the public OMIM entry could guide which supplied facts a draft selects. Provenance checks cannot detect this, so stated-fact coverage on older entries may be inflated.

Additional limitation to state explicitly: attrition from the safety filter may be correlated with disease content, making the compared subset non-random. The interesting large-entry regime is entirely unevaluated.
Additional limitation to state explicitly: the benchmark's discriminative power among strategies is near the noise floor in the tested regime, limiting its value as a leaderboard-style benchmark.
